title: 7 Best Concrete Oil Stain Removers in 2026: Pick by Stain Age
metaDescription: Terminator-HSD is the best concrete oil stain remover for old, set-in stains; Pour-N-Restore suits weeks-old spots and Oil Eater handles fresh drips.

intro:
The best concrete oil stain remover for old, set-in stains is Terminator-HSD, a microbial cleaner that digests oil inside the pores instead of just washing the surface. For stains a few weeks or months old, Pour-N-Restore pulls oil out like a poultice, and for fresh drips, Oil-Dri absorbent followed by Oil Eater degreaser usually leaves nothing behind.

No single product wins on every stain, because a fresh puddle, a months-old drip and a decade-old garage floor halo need different chemistry. Below are seven removers ranked by what each handles best, the four product families explained, how to match a product to your stain, and what works on asphalt and pavers. Rankings are based on manufacturer directions, label claims, product chemistry and recurring owner feedback, not hands-on trials.
quickAnswer: Buy by stain age. Fresh spill: Oil-Dri granules, then Oil Eater or Chomp!. Weeks to months old: Pour-N-Restore or a homemade diatomaceous earth poultice. Years old and faded: Terminator-HSD kept damp for one to two weeks. Finish with a whole-slab wash such as Zep so treated spots blend in.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Concrete Oil Stain Removers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
### Best for Old Stains: Terminator-HSD Microbial Oil Stain Remover

Terminator-HSD is a powder you mix with water and brush into the stain. Instead of emulsifying oil for a rinse, it delivers hydrocarbon-digesting microbes that break the oil down where it sits, which is why it reaches stains that degreasers only lighten. The maker positions it for old, set-in oil on concrete, asphalt and pavers. The routine is easy but patient: clean the surface, apply the mix, keep the area damp and do not rinse for the time on the label. Owners commonly report that a stain looks unchanged for a few days and then fades over the following week or two. It works best when the concrete is above roughly 50 degrees Fahrenheit and slows sharply in a cold garage. Because it contains no solvents, it is one of the few strong options that is safe on blacktop. Keep bleach and disinfecting cleaners off the area before and during treatment, because they kill the microbes.

**Pros:** Breaks oil down in place instead of lifting only the top layer; water-based and suitable for asphalt; keeps working in the pores; powder concentrate stores well.

**Cons:** Slow, often days to a couple of weeks; needs moisture and warmth; weak on fresh puddles that were not absorbed first.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Terminator-HSD+oil+stain+remover&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Poultice: Pour-N-Restore Oil Stain Remover

Pour-N-Restore is a poultice in a bottle. You pour the liquid onto a dry stain, brush it out so it covers the stain plus about an inch beyond, and let it dry. As it dries it turns into a white powder that has drawn oil up out of the pores, and you sweep or vacuum it away. The label lists concrete, asphalt and pavers, and owners commonly praise how little scrubbing it takes. It is most effective on stains a few weeks to a few months old, where oil has sunk below a degreaser's reach but not deep into the slab. Old garage floor stains usually need several applications, and the directions allow repeating it. Drying time depends on temperature and humidity, so plan on most of a day in cool weather. It costs more per stain than a homemade diatomaceous earth poultice, but you never have to guess at the mix or the consistency.

**Pros:** Dries to a powder that pulls oil from the pores; very little scrubbing; label covers concrete, asphalt and pavers; strong on medium-age stains.

**Cons:** Needs hours to dry before sweeping; one round rarely clears a deep stain; costs more per stain than a homemade poultice.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Pour-N-Restore+Oil+Stain+Remover&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Degreaser: Oil Eater Original Cleaner Degreaser Concentrate

Oil Eater Original is a water-based alkaline degreaser concentrate that has been on garage shelves for years. The label gives dilutions from light cleaning up to near full strength for heavy grease, so one jug covers everything from washing a whole driveway to attacking a fresh drip. On pre-wet concrete, scrubbed with a stiff brush and given a short dwell, it emulsifies oil so a rinse carries it away, and it runs through many pressure washer detergent systems. Its limit is depth. On stains that have sat in concrete for months it cleans the top, and the mark often wicks back as the slab dries; that is where pairing it with a poultice or enzyme product pays off. Owners commonly use it as step one in a stain routine and as a whole-floor cleaner before sealing or coating. It is non-flammable but alkaline, so wear gloves and eye protection.

**Pros:** Concentrate dilutes from light cleaning to heavy grease; brush or pressure washer; water-based and non-flammable; inexpensive per gallon of mix.

**Cons:** Removes surface and shallow oil, not deep stains; can leave a lighter patch on its own; needs a thorough rinse.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Oil+Eater+Original+Cleaner+Degreaser&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Ready-to-Use: Chomp! Oil and Grease Stain Remover

Chomp! is a ready-to-use oil and grease stain remover sold for driveways, garage floors and other concrete. It suits anyone who wants a bottle on the shelf that works straight away, with nothing to measure. The label routine is the familiar one: blot or absorb free oil, apply, agitate with a stiff brush, let it sit and rinse with a hose. On fresh drips and stains a few days old, owners commonly report clean results in one or two rounds. On old, dark garage floor stains it behaves like any surface degreaser, lightening the mark without clearing what sits deep in the slab, so follow it with a poultice or enzyme product. Because it is sold ready-mixed, the cost per square foot is higher than a concentrate, which makes it better for spot work than for washing a whole driveway. On asphalt, check the current label and test a small corner first.

**Pros:** No mixing; formulated for driveway and garage concrete; handy for spot treatments on fresh drips; brush and hose rinse is all it needs.

**Cons:** Small bottles get expensive on big jobs; limited effect on very old stains; check the label before using on asphalt.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Chomp+Oil+and+Grease+Stain+Remover&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Whole Driveways: Zep Driveway and Concrete Cleaner Concentrate

Zep's concentrate is built for whole-surface cleaning rather than single stains. It runs through a pressure washer's detergent system or a pump sprayer and targets the general mix of tire marks, dirt, light oil and organic grime that makes concrete look dingy. That makes it a useful second product in an oil stain project. Once you have treated individual stains, washing the entire driveway removes the contrast between the freshly cleaned spots and the rest of the slab, which otherwise dry noticeably lighter. On its own, it lightens recent drips and handles very light stains but is not aggressive enough for heavy or old ones. Follow the label dilution, apply from the bottom of the slope up to avoid streaks, keep it wet through the dwell and rinse with a surface cleaner or wide tip. It is commonly sold in gallon jugs at home centers, and one jug typically treats a two-car driveway.

**Pros:** Made for pressure washer use; cleans general grime and light oil together; large jugs keep cost per square foot low; evens out color after spot work.

**Cons:** Not strong enough alone for heavy oil; best with a pressure washer; can lighten concrete unevenly if used only in spots.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Zep+Driveway+and+Concrete+Cleaner+Concentrate&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget: Purple Power Industrial Strength Degreaser

Purple Power Industrial Strength is a heavy-duty alkaline degreaser sold at auto parts stores and home centers at a low cost per gallon. It is aggressive on fresh oil and grease and doubles as a general garage floor cleaner when diluted to the label rate. The strength that makes it effective also calls for care. Highly alkaline cleaners can dull aluminum, darken some metals and haze certain acrylic sealers, so keep it off wheels and trim and test sealed or stamped concrete first. Wear gloves and eye protection, and open the garage door for ventilation. On stains, use it like any degreaser: absorb free oil, pre-wet the slab, apply, scrub, keep it from drying and rinse thoroughly. Like the other degreasers here, it handles the top layer and shallow oil but will not pull a stain that has moved deep into the concrete. If price decides it, this is the one to buy.

**Pros:** Very low cost per gallon; strong on fresh grease and oil; easy to find at auto parts stores; works as a whole-floor garage cleaner.

**Cons:** Highly alkaline, which can affect aluminum and some sealers; strong odor indoors; same depth limits as other degreasers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Purple+Power+Industrial+Strength+Degreaser&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Fresh Spills: Oil-Dri Clay Absorbent

Oil-Dri makes clay absorbent granules for garages, shops and driveways. They are the first line of defense rather than a stain remover in the strict sense. Spread over a fresh spill and ground in with a shoe or a brick, they soak up free oil before it wicks into the concrete, and that single step often decides whether a spill becomes a permanent stain. The granules are safe on every driveway surface, including asphalt, because there is no chemistry involved. Leave them several hours or overnight, then sweep them up and dispose of them according to local rules for oily waste. They do nothing for stains that have already dried and set, so pair them with a degreaser, poultice or enzyme product for older spots. You can also grind them to a fine powder and mix them with degreaser to make a homemade poultice. A large bag lasts years in most garages.

**Pros:** Pulls up free oil before it soaks in; inexpensive, large bags last years; safe on concrete, asphalt and pavers; doubles as traction on icy steps.

**Cons:** Does nothing for old, set-in stains; needs grinding in and hours of contact; used granules must be disposed of as oily waste.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Oil-Dri+Clay+Absorbent&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: What Are the Four Types of Oil Stain Remover?
sections.body:
Every product on the shelf fits one of four families, and the family explains most of the difference in results.

| Family | Best for | Speed | Asphalt-safe | Relative cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Absorbent | Fresh spills | Hours | Yes | Lowest |
| Degreaser | Fresh to weeks-old | Minutes | Water-based only | Low |
| Poultice | Weeks to months old | 1-2 days per round | Usually; check label | Moderate |
| Enzyme / microbial | Months to years old | Days to weeks | Yes | Moderate |

### Absorbents

Clay granules, diatomaceous earth and sawdust physically soak up liquid oil. They are cheap and safe on any surface but only help while oil is still liquid and near the top.

### Degreasers

Alkaline or surfactant cleaners emulsify oil so water can carry it away. They work only on what they touch during a 5 to 15 minute dwell, so they clean the top fraction of an inch and leave deeper oil behind.

### Poultices

An absorbent powder mixed with an oil-dissolving liquid. As the liquid evaporates upward it carries oil into the powder, which reaches deeper than any degreaser.

### Enzyme and microbial cleaners

Microbes break hydrocarbons down into carbon dioxide and water and keep working in the pores after you walk away. They are slow, need moisture and warmth, and are the gentlest option around asphalt, plants and pets.

sections.heading: Which Oil Stain Remover Should You Use on Your Stain?
sections.body:
Look at the stain, and do one quick test, before you shop.

### The paper towel test

Press a paper towel onto the stain and stand on it for a minute. An oily ring means free oil is still near the surface, so absorbent plus degreaser is your first move. A clean towel on a dark stain means the oil is in the slab, and you can skip straight to a poultice or enzyme product.

### Fresh, shiny and slick

Put granules down right away, grind them in, leave them overnight, then scrub the rest with Oil Eater or Chomp!. On fresh spills this combination commonly leaves nothing visible. The full fresh-spill routine for both blacktop and concrete is in our guide on [how to remove oil stains from a driveway](/how-to-remove-oil-stains-from-driveway/).

### Dark and dull, weeks or months old

Degrease once and let it dry. If it fades a lot, repeat. If it barely changes, the oil is below a degreaser's reach, and Pour-N-Restore or a homemade poultice will usually take it most of the way out in two or three rounds.

### A big faded halo, years old

This is old oil spread through the slab, typical of a garage floor or long-term parking spot. An enzyme cleaner like Terminator-HSD is the efficient choice here, because covering a four-foot halo in poultice uses a lot of material. Keep it damp and give it a week or more.

### Many stains plus general grime

Budget for a whole-surface wash like Zep after the spot work so the slab dries to one even color. Our [best driveway cleaner](/best-driveway-cleaner/) roundup covers that broader job, including rust and mildew.

sections.heading: How Do You Get the Best Results From an Oil Stain Remover?
sections.body:
Most failed stain jobs fail on technique, not product.

### Remove free oil first

Even a stain that looks dry can hold oil in its surface texture. A quick pass with absorbent catches it before any liquid product goes down.

### Pre-wet before degreasing

Dry concrete drinks cleaner instantly and can pull emulsified oil deeper. A lightly damp surface keeps the action near the top where you can rinse it away.

### Scrub with weight behind it

A stiff nylon or polypropylene brush on a pole forces cleaner into the pores and breaks the oil film. Skip wire brushes on decorative concrete and asphalt. Keep the cleaner wet through its dwell, misting in sun or wind.

### Rinse well and judge dry

A pressure washer with a 25 degree tip or a surface cleaner flushes emulsified oil out better than a hose; our guide to the [best surface cleaner for a pressure washer](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) explains why. Then let the concrete dry 24 to 48 hours before deciding whether to repeat.

### Different rules for poultices and enzymes

Poultices should dry slowly under plastic for a day or two. Enzymes need moisture and no rinsing for the label period. Neither benefits from scrubbing once applied. The step-by-step methods for deep stains are in our guide on [how to get oil out of concrete](/how-to-get-oil-out-of-concrete/).

sections.heading: Which Oil Stain Removers Are Safe on Asphalt and Pavers?
sections.body:
Many driveway oil removers assume concrete, so check the label before using one on anything else.

### Asphalt

Asphalt binder is a heavy petroleum product, and solvents that dissolve motor oil also soften the pavement. Water-based degreasers, enzyme cleaners and absorbents are generally safe; solvent and citrus solvent products are not. Of the picks here, Terminator-HSD and Oil-Dri are the most clearly asphalt-friendly because they involve no solvents, and Pour-N-Restore lists asphalt on its label. Keep highly alkaline products such as Purple Power for concrete. If oil has already softened a blacktop spot, clean it, prime it with an oil spot primer and seal; our [asphalt driveway sealer reviews](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) cover that step.

### Pavers

What is the best product to get oil off pavers? A poultice such as Pour-N-Restore or an enzyme cleaner, because the sand joints soak up oil and wash out under high pressure. Treat both the paver face and the joint, rinse gently and top up joint sand afterward. A heavily stained paver can also be lifted and flipped.

### Pressure on any surface

A narrow tip at close range strips fine aggregate from asphalt and etches concrete. Use a wide tip, stay about a foot away and keep moving.

sections.heading: What Household Products Remove Oil From Concrete?
sections.body:
A few kitchen-cabinet options work; most do not.

### Worth using

- Dish soap is a real, if mild, degreaser. Scrubbed in and left 15 minutes, it handles fresh spills and is safe on asphalt.
- Plain clay kitty litter is close to a commercial absorbent and a perfectly good first response.
- A homemade poultice of diatomaceous earth or finely ground clay litter mixed with a strong degreaser, spread a quarter inch thick and covered with plastic for a day or two, works on the same principle as bottled poultices for a few dollars.

### Not worth it

- Cola lifts a little surface grime but does not dissolve oil and leaves sugar that attracts dirt and insects.
- WD-40 loosens fresh grease but adds more petroleum to clean up.
- Bleach lightens mildew, not oil.
- Muriatic acid etches concrete and can leave a bright ring around an unchanged stain.
- Oven cleaner is strongly alkaline and does break down grease, but it is harsh on skin, can discolor concrete and costs far more per square foot than a degreaser concentrate.

### Is TSP good for oil stains?

Trisodium phosphate is a strong alkaline cleaner that degreases concrete much like the products above and is often used before painting. It is caustic, phosphates are restricted in some areas, and it should be rinsed well and kept out of drains and beds.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Protection for Concrete From Oil Stains?
sections.body:
Seal the slab once it is clean and dry, catch the drips and keep a spill kit handy.

### Penetrating sealer

A silane or siloxane penetrating sealer reduces how quickly oil soaks in without changing the look. It will not make concrete stainproof, but it buys time to blot a spill before it sets. Confirm the slab is ready first: water sprinkled on it should soak in evenly. Our [concrete driveway sealer reviews](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/) focus on exterior slabs.

### Garage floor coating

In a garage, an epoxy or polyaspartic coating seals the floor completely so oil sits on top and wipes off. Coatings fail over oil, so they demand thorough degreasing and surface prep first, which is where these removers earn their keep. See our [best garage floor epoxy](/best-garage-floor-epoxy/) picks.

### Drip pans and a spill kit

A containment mat or drip pan placed under the engine, not where you guess the engine sits, catches slow leaks. Keep absorbent granules, a stiff brush and a jug of degreaser by the garage door, and get the leak fixed, because a steady drip overwhelms any sealer.

### Safety and runoff

Alkaline degreasers are caustic in concentrate, so wear gloves and safety glasses. Treat any solvent poultice as a fire hazard and ventilate. Rinse water carries oil and cleaner residue, so keep it out of storm drains by rinsing onto gravel or lawn where allowed, berming the drain or collecting it with a wet vacuum.

mistakes.title: Using a Degreaser on a Years-Old Stain
mistakes.body: Degreasers only reach oil near the surface during their short dwell. On a stain that has been in the slab for years they clean the top, and the mark returns as the concrete dries. Switch to a poultice or enzyme cleaner instead of buying a stronger degreaser.

mistakes.title: Skipping the Absorbent on Fresh Spills
mistakes.body: Cleaner poured onto a puddle emulsifies the oil and spreads it over a larger area, sometimes driving it deeper. Pull up free oil with granules first, grind them in and wait several hours. Every product works better once the loose oil is gone.

mistakes.title: Rinsing an Enzyme Cleaner Too Soon
mistakes.body: Microbial products need time and moisture to digest oil. Rinsing after an hour or letting the spot dry out stops them early. Follow the no-rinse period on the label, keep the area damp and wait at least a week before deciding it failed.

mistakes.title: Using Concrete Products on Asphalt Without Checking
mistakes.body: Solvent-based and highly alkaline cleaners can soften asphalt binder or leave pale patches, and many driveway products assume concrete. Look for an asphalt statement on the label, test a small corner and favor enzyme cleaners and absorbents on blacktop.

mistakes.title: Sending Wash Water Into the Storm Drain
mistakes.body: Rinse water from stain removal carries oil and cleaner residue, and storm drains usually flow straight to streams. Many towns restrict it. Rinse onto gravel or lawn where allowed, berm off the drain or collect the water with a wet vacuum.

faqs.q: What is the best concrete oil stain remover?
faqs.a: It depends on the stain age. For old, set-in stains, Terminator-HSD is the best pick because its microbes digest oil inside the pores. For weeks-old stains, Pour-N-Restore works like a poultice. For fresh spills, Oil-Dri granules followed by Oil Eater degreaser usually leave nothing behind. Matching the product to the stain matters more than the brand.

faqs.q: What is the best old oil stain remover for concrete?
faqs.a: An enzyme or microbial cleaner such as Terminator-HSD, or repeated poultice rounds with Pour-N-Restore or homemade diatomaceous earth paste. Old oil sits well below the surface, so degreasers alone keep failing. Expect three to five poultice rounds or one to two weeks of enzyme treatment, and judge each round on fully dry concrete.

faqs.q: Do enzyme oil stain removers really work on garage floors?
faqs.a: Yes, on the right stain and with patience. Microbial cleaners break oil down in place, so they reach stains degreasers cannot. Owners commonly report gradual fading over one to two weeks. They work poorly in cold garages below roughly 50 degrees Fahrenheit, on surfaces treated with bleach or acid, and on puddles that were not absorbed first.

faqs.q: What absorbs oil on concrete best?
faqs.a: Clay granules such as Oil-Dri or plain non-clumping kitty litter, ground in with a shoe and left overnight, are the best quick absorbents for fresh spills. Diatomaceous earth is even more porous and is the top choice for a homemade poultice. Sawdust, cornmeal and baking soda work in a pinch but hold less oil per pound.

faqs.q: Can you mix two oil stain removers together?
faqs.a: No. Use products in sequence instead: absorbent, then degreaser, then a poultice or enzyme cleaner if needed. Rinse thoroughly between chemical products, especially before an enzyme treatment, because degreaser residue can harm the microbes. Never combine any cleaner with bleach, which can release toxic gas with some products and does nothing for oil anyway.

faqs.q: Will a pressure washer alone remove oil from concrete?
faqs.a: Rarely. Cold water does not dissolve oil, so a pressure washer by itself mostly cleans around the stain. It is excellent as a rinse after a degreaser or poultice, flushing emulsified oil out of the surface texture. Hot water units are far more effective on oil, which is why commercial cleaning crews use them.

faqs.q: How many applications does an oil stain usually need?
faqs.a: Fresh spills usually need one round of absorbent plus degreaser. Stains a few weeks old often take two or three degreaser or poultice rounds. Old garage floor stains may need three to five poultice applications or one to two weeks of enzyme treatment. Judge each round only after the concrete has dried for a full day.

bottomLine: Buy by stain age. Keep Oil-Dri granules and a degreaser concentrate such as Oil Eater, or Purple Power on a budget, ready for fresh spills, reach for Pour-N-Restore or a homemade diatomaceous earth poultice when a stain has had weeks to set, and use Terminator-HSD for old, faded garage floor halos you can leave alone for a week or two. Whatever you use, absorb first, keep cleaners wet while they work, judge on dry concrete and keep runoff out of the drain. Then seal the slab and fix the leak so you only do this once.
